runs.label: Degree-two rotation · independent solver comparison
runs.summary: Three calculations with two independent numerical methods start from the same requested degree-two harmonic coefficients with Ω=3. Over a full period, the amplitude-inclusive P₂ψ error in the prescribed rotating frame falls from 1.83% at Fortran NG48 to 0.678% at NG100; independent harmonic JAX gives 1.3×10⁻¹⁴. No rotation rate is fitted. The raw profile propagates with speed −1 in this frame, or 2 in the inertial frame. This is a test of the exact solution and numerical accuracy, not evidence that turbulence approaches it.

figures.alt: Degree-two moving-frame profile and amplitude errors at two grid resolutions and in JAX
figures.caption: Only degree two is compared, including amplitude. Each curve uses its own initial profile; separate comparisons below include the small initial differences from discrete sampling, mean compatibility correction and Poisson inversion.

figures.alt: Degree-two motion in the original frame and persistence after removing the predicted rotation
figures.caption: The same spectral degree-two field moves in the recorded frame and is steady in its prescribed moving frame. The diagnostic retains amplitude and does not fit the propagation speed.

runs.label: Shared turbulent initial field · independent methods
runs.summary: With Ω=3, both methods start from the same requested harmonic vorticity in degrees 4–6, without amplitude rescaling. At t=10, Fortran NG100 and harmonic JAX L127 put 92.1% and 90.9% of their energy in degree two. Their amplitude-inclusive P₂ profiles differ by 17.7%, while halving the Fortran time step changes its P₂ profile by only 0.0578%. Spatial refinement remains essential: neither method is a converged reference, and the prescribed rotation is never fitted to the data. The Fortran sampling compatibility correction is disclosed.

figures.alt: Independent Fortran and harmonic degree-two comparison
figures.caption: Same requested initial harmonics, amplitude retained, no fitted phase. The early difference includes discrete projection and inversion. Angular momentum and other degrees are excluded from the P₂ profile distance.

figures.alt: Fortran mixed-run time-step refinement
figures.caption: Reducing CFL from 0.05 to 0.025 changes the final degree-two profile by 0.0578%. This isolates time-step sensitivity at NG100.

runs.label: Harmonic refinement · conservation is not resolution
runs.summary: The same mixed-degree initial field gives E₂/E=0.814, 0.898 and 0.909 at harmonic cutoffs L31, L63 and L127. At a common time step, the final P₂ difference falls from 67.2% for L31→L63 to 19.8% for L63→L127. Halving the L127 time step changes P₂ by only 0.00176%. These finite-time results separate truncation sensitivity from time integration; they do not establish continuum convergence or long-time freezing. At L127, roughly 36% of enstrophy occupies the upper third of retained degrees. High-degree enstrophy accumulation is expected in truncated-equilibrium theory; it is not by itself a numerical failure. The distinction is between accurately solving each finite truncation and establishing a limit as the cutoff increases.

figures.alt: Comparison of degree-two profiles at L63 and L127
figures.caption: Both calculations use dt=0.001. Truncation still materially affects the degree-two profile by t=10.

figures.alt: L127 time-step refinement
figures.caption: At fixed L127, halving dt from 0.001 to 0.0005 gives a much smaller profile difference. Small invariant drift alone does not ensure spatial resolution.

runs.label: CPU and GPU · same numerical experiment
runs.summary: At identical L63, dt=0.001, shared initial coefficients and 64-bit precision, CPU and NVIDIA A100 runs agree to about 3.2×10⁻¹¹ in the final amplitude-inclusive P₂ profile. This checks device consistency. It does not test spectral truncation or a turbulent end state.

runs.label: Independent spectral solver · CPU and GPU validation
runs.summary: All 17 spectral and runner tests passed in each Unity allocation. At L=63, 100 warm JAX steps took 3.705 s on the CPU allocation and 0.06074 s on the GPU allocation. The same equations and inputs were used at each L. An A100 allocation was requested and CUDA execution was recorded; the model string was not logged. These are separate-hardware, single-observation timings, excluding compilation and output, and do not measure speedup over Fortran or long-time flow behavior.

figures.alt: Measured warm and first-compilation times of the independent spectral solver on separate Unity CPU and CUDA GPU allocations at degrees 15, 31, and 63.
figures.caption: Warm advancement is synchronized and excludes compilation, host transfer, diagnostics, and file output. Startup cost is shown separately. Same method and inputs at each L; different CPU and GPU allocations.

runs.label: Figure 5 protocol · NG200 viscous and inviscid pair
runs.summary: Six snapshots span one prescribed degree-six Rossby–Haurwitz period with Ω=50 about y. The inviscid recurrence shape error is 1.120%, down from 11.61% at NG48. A separate end-point phase fit gives a 0.03027% cycle offset; the plotted recurrence is not phase-corrected. The legacy-viscous row retains 98.16% of its projected amplitude. Its grid-dependent viscosity is smaller than at NG48, so the damping change is not a fixed-viscosity convergence test. This is a new seeded realization.

figures.alt: NG200 viscous and inviscid relative-vorticity fields at six times spanning one predicted degree-six wave period.
figures.caption: Top: legacy Laplacian viscosity. Bottom: inviscid. Six recorded times use a shared color scale; the last column is the prescribed first recurrence, without fitted rotation.

runs.label: Time-step refinement · same initial fields
runs.summary: The two NG100 runs begin with byte-identical grids and sampled fields. Halving the time-step factor reduces enstrophy drift by 15.5 times. Their degree-two amplitudes remain close while their late-time profiles separate. Chaotic trajectory separation alone is not a convergence verdict; the strong drift reduction is direct evidence that the original time step needs refinement. This comparison tests only P₂ψ and monitors degree one separately.

figures.alt: Degree-two profile, amplitude, and energy comparison under time-step refinement
figures.caption: Common saved times without interpolation or fitted rotation. The profile difference retains amplitude; normalized pattern difference and amplitude ratio are displayed separately. Ω=0 gives zero prescribed speed.

runs.label: Figure 5 protocol · coarse viscous and inviscid pair
runs.summary: Six snapshots through one prescribed Rossby–Haurwitz period, with degree 6 and rotation Ω=50 about y. The upper row uses the original Laplacian viscosity; the lower row is inviscid. The inviscid field returns with an 11.6% shape error on this coarse grid. A separate end-point phase fit attributes most of the mismatch to a 0.43% cycle offset; plotted prescribed-speed errors remain unfitted. This tests the protocol, not convergence at the paper resolution.

figures.alt: Viscous and inviscid wave fields at six times
figures.caption: Top: legacy Laplacian viscosity. Bottom: inviscid. Columns span one predicted rotating-frame period; fixed color scale preserves the damping comparison.

runs.label: Figure 6 protocol · coarse-grid pilot
runs.summary: Unity pilot with initially equal discrete energy in degrees 4, 5 and 6. Degree-two energy grows to 88.9%, while its normalized coefficients keep changing. This coarse grid has 2.2% enstrophy drift and measurable degree-one leakage; it is a validation pilot, not a converged reproduction or evidence of an asymptotic state.

runs.label: Long-time extension · coarse-grid stress test
runs.summary: Degree two retains 88.6% of the energy at t=600, but its normalized coefficients and its rotation-invariant shape keep changing. Persistence times do not grow monotonically across the sampled ages. Energy increases 1.17%, enstrophy increases 22.29%, and degree one acquires 2.31% of the energy. These numerical errors preclude a conclusion about a continuum end state or statistical symmetry restoration.
